hook.text: Count every word in Jane Austen's Emma, and rank them from most common to least.

top.text: Top of the list is the little word to, five thousand two hundred and thirty-nine times.

cliff.text: On plain axes, the counts fall off a cliff.

scroll.text: And then the ranks just keep going, all the way out to seven thousand and seventy-nine.

tail.text: More than half of those words lie flat along the floor. They're used once or twice.

switch.text: Now switch both axes to a log scale, where each step is ten times the last.

straight.text: The curve straightens into a line. That straight line is Zipf's law.

law.text: It's one over the rank: go ten times further down the list, and a word turns up a tenth as often.

slope.text: That's a slope of minus one: one step down for every step along.

predict.text: So the law makes a prediction.

real.text: In Emma, the second word, the, turns up five thousand two hundred and one times. It nearly ties with to.

rough.text: And the tenth, she, comes in at more than four times its prediction.

warn.text: Log axes show the shape, but they're bad at shares.

plain.text: On a plain one, they're one point four percent of the vocabulary.

top100.text: Count the text they fill instead, and those hundred words are sixty percent of the book.

once.text: And of its seven thousand and seventy-nine different words, thirty-nine percent appear only once.

why.text: That lopsided split is why stopwords exist: a few words fill most of the text, and they say the least about it.

stop.text: Seventy of Emma's top hundred are on NLTK's stopword list.

idf.text: And it's why IDF, inverse document frequency, gives a word more weight the fewer documents it turns up in.

fit.text: Fit a line to the top thousand words, and its slope comes out at minus one point one four.

anchor.text: Start from the top word: the second should turn up half as often, and the tenth, a tenth as often.

crowd.text: The top words crowd together, so the law is rough at the very top.

logaxis.text: On a log rank axis, the top hundred words fill half the width, as if they were half the vocabulary.
